Here's how I'd think about airfoil alternatives for a 2m wingspan UAV carrying up to 5kg payload:

## Why look beyond NACA 0012

NACA 0012 is symmetric, which means zero lift at zero angle of attack. That's fine for aerobatic aircraft or tail surfaces, but for a payload-carrying UAV cruising at a fixed angle, you're forcing a higher AoA (and more induced drag) to generate the lift you need. A cambered airfoil generates lift more efficiently at your cruise condition.

## Suggested airfoils to compare in your CFD study

**Clark Y**
A classic choice for small UAVs and RC aircraft. Flat bottom (easy to manufacture/build), moderate camber, good lift-to-drag ratio, gentle stall characteristics. Very well documented — lots of published Cl/Cd data to validate your CFD against.

**Eppler E205 / E212**
Designed specifically for low Reynolds number applications (which is exactly the regime a 2m UAV flying at modest speeds operates in). Good lift coefficients at low drag.

**SD7062 / SD7037 (Selig-Donovan series)**
Purpose-built for low-Re UAV and RC applications by Michael Selig's group at UIUC. SD7062 in particular is popular for higher-lift, payload-carrying small UAVs. Extensive wind tunnel data available from the UIUC Airfoil Database for validation.

**NACA 4412 or NACA 2412**
If you want to stay within the NACA family for design familiarity, these cambered 4-digit airfoils give you real lift at reasonable AoA, with well-understood behavior and easy parametric generation.

**MH-series (Martin Hepperle) — e.g., MH32, MH45**
Optimized for RC gliders/UAVs, good glide performance, low drag.

## What matters most for your case

Since you're payload-limited (5 kg) and presumably want decent endurance:
- **Reynolds number** — calculate your operating Re first (depends on chord length and cruise speed); airfoil performance is very Re-dependent, so pick airfoils validated near your actual Re, not just at high-Re conditions
- **Higher max Cl** — helps if you want a smaller wing or slower stall speed for payload drops/landing
- **L/D ratio at cruise** — directly impacts endurance/range
- **Manufacturability** — flat-bottom airfoils (Clark Y) are easier to build for composite/foam construction

## For your CFD workflow

I'd suggest running NACA 0012 as your baseline (control case, since it's heavily documented for validating your mesh/solver setup), then comparing against **Clark Y** and **SD7062** as your two cambered candidates — that gives you a manufacturability-focused option and a performance-optimized option to weigh against each other.

**In DesignModeler specifically**

Here's a lean meshing strategy that keeps cell count reasonable while still capturing the physics you need (boundary layer, tip vortex, wake).

## 1. Overall approach

Use a **hybrid mesh**: unstructured tetrahedral/polyhedral in the bulk domain, with **prism/inflation layers** on the wing surface for the boundary layer. This gives you good BL resolution without the cell count explosion of a fully structured hex mesh on a curved 3D wing.

## 2. Boundary layer (inflation) — this is where accuracy actually comes from

- **First layer height**: calculate from your target y+. For most CFD with a turbulence model like **k-ω SST** (good default for wings, handles adverse pressure gradients well), aim for **y+ ≈ 1** if you want to resolve the viscous sublayer directly, or **y+ ≈ 30-50** if you're using wall functions and want to save cells.
  - For a first pass to save compute, y+ ~30-50 with wall functions is a reasonable trade-off. Go y+~1 later if you need more accuracy near stall.
- **Number of inflation layers**: 15-20 layers is typical, with a **growth rate of 1.15-1.2** to smoothly transition into the bulk mesh.
- Apply inflation only on the **wing surface** named selection — not on farfield or symmetry faces.

## 3. Bulk mesh sizing (keep cells low here)

- Use **body sizing / face sizing controls** rather than uniformly refining the whole domain:
  - Fine mesh near the wing surface and wake region
  - Coarser mesh as you move toward the farfield boundaries (this is where most cell savings come from — don't waste resolution 15 chord-lengths away from the wing)
- Use a **growth rate of ~1.2** from fine to coarse regions so the transition isn't abrupt (abrupt jumps cause numerical diffusion/error)

## 4. Local refinement zones (this is the key to "clean but not huge")

- **Wingtip region**: add a local refinement (sphere of influence or body of influence) around the tip to resolve the tip vortex — this is usually the single biggest accuracy bottleneck in 3D wing CFD if under-resolved
- **Wake region**: a body of influence extending downstream of the trailing edge (a box or cylinder shape) with moderate refinement, since the wake needs decent resolution to capture drag accurately
- **Leading edge**: slightly finer face sizing here since curvature is high and this is where flow acceleration/pressure gradients are steepest

## 5. Practical cell count target

For a single half-wing (with symmetry), a clean mesh that balances accuracy and compute is typically in the range of:
- **1.5-4 million cells** for RANS with wall functions
- Higher (5-8M+) if you push toward y+~1 and want to resolve stall behavior accurately

Start on the lower end, check your **Cl/Cd convergence and y+ contour** on the wing surface, and refine locally only where needed rather than uniformly bumping global mesh density.

## 6. Mesh quality checks before running

- **Orthogonal quality** > 0.1 (higher is better, aim for >0.15-0.2 minimum, ideally >0.3 average)
- **Skewness** < 0.95 (ideally most cells < 0.7)
- **Aspect ratio** in inflation layers can be high (that's expected/fine near the wall) but check it doesn't degrade quality elsewhere

Here's what to set for inflation specifically — geometry selection and boundary type matter a lot for getting it to actually apply correctly.

## Geometry (what body/faces to select)

- **Geometry field**: select the **fluid domain body** (the one you got after the Boolean subtract) — inflation is a body-level mesh control, applied on the volume that touches the surface you want layers on.
- **Boundary field**: select the **wing surface** named selection (all faces of the wing — upper surface, lower surface, tip cap if you modeled a blunt tip, leading and trailing edges). This is the actual surface the prism layers grow *from*.

Do **not** apply inflation on:
- The symmetry plane face
- The farfield/inlet/outlet faces
- Any far-domain walls

Inflation should only originate from solid, no-slip wall surfaces — physically, that's the only place a boundary layer exists.

## Inflation Option (in Ansys Meshing, under Details of Inflation)

Most common choices:

1. **Smooth Transition** (recommended default) — automatically sets layer count based on local surface mesh size and growth rate, adapts to curvature better on complex 3D geometry like a wing. Easiest to get a clean result without manual tuning.
2. **Total Thickness** — you specify total BL thickness and number of layers directly; more control but requires you to already know your estimated BL thickness (from a flat-plate approximation, roughly δ ≈ 0.37x/Re_x^0.2 for turbulent flow).
3. **First Layer Thickness** — you directly input the y+-derived first cell height (this is the one you'll want once you've calculated y+ from your Reynolds number) plus number of layers and growth rate.

For your case, once you've calculated first-layer height from your target y+, use **First Layer Thickness** so you have direct control of the wall-adjacent cell size — this is the more rigorous approach for aerodynamic accuracy.

## Settings to pair with it

- **Growth rate**: 1.15-1.2
- **Max layers**: 15-20 (as discussed earlier)
- **Inflation algorithm**: **Post** (post-inflation, default and generally more robust) vs Pre — stick with Post unless you're having mesh generation failures, then Pre can sometimes help with complex geometry

## One common issue to watch for

On a 3D wing, the **wingtip region and leading edge** (high curvature areas) are where inflation most commonly fails or produces bad quality cells (layer collapse, spikes). If you see this after meshing:
- Reduce growth rate slightly (e.g., 1.1) in that zone
- Or use a **local inflation control** with adjusted settings just for the tip, separate from the main wing surface control

speaker: Claude
chat:
Yes, k-ω SST is a solid choice for this. Here's the reasoning and what to check:

## Why k-ω SST works well here

- It blends k-ω near the wall (good for boundary layer and adverse pressure gradient prediction — important since you'll see this near stall/high AoA) with k-ε in the freestream (good far-field behavior, less sensitive to inlet turbulence assumptions)
- Well validated for **external aerodynamics on wings/airfoils**, especially when you care about separation prediction, stall behavior, and Cl/Cd accuracy
- Performs better than standard k-ε for flows with curvature and pressure gradients, which a wing definitely has

## First, check your Reynolds number at 30 m/s

This actually matters for whether k-ω SST alone is sufficient, or whether you need a **transition model** on top of it.

Quick estimate: Re = (ρ × V × c) / μ

At sea level, ρ ≈ 1.225 kg/m³, μ ≈ 1.8×10⁻⁵ Pa·s

If your **chord length** is, say, 0.3m: Re ≈ (1.225 × 30 × 0.3) / 1.8×10⁻⁵ ≈ **612,000**

That's a fairly typical small-UAV Reynolds number — you're in a regime where **laminar-to-turbulent transition matters** (unlike large aircraft where flow is basically fully turbulent everywhere). Standard k-ω SST assumes fully turbulent flow from the leading edge, which can **over-predict drag and miss laminar separation bubbles** that are common at this Re range.

## Recommendation

Consider **k-ω SST with the Transition SST (γ-Reθ) model** (also called "Transition SST" in Fluent) instead of plain k-ω SST, if your Re is in the 200k-1,000,000 range. This is a meaningful accuracy improvement for small UAV wings specifically, since:
- It captures laminar separation bubbles
- More accurate Cl/Cd prediction at the Re your UAV actually operates at
- Standard k-ω SST alone tends to trip the flow to turbulent too early, which can under-predict drag issues near stall

The trade-off: Transition SST is a bit more sensitive to mesh quality near the leading edge and needs finer resolution there, plus it typically needs a well-resolved **y+~1** mesh (not wall functions) to work properly.

## Practical suggestion

- **First pass / mesh validation**: run plain k-ω SST with wall functions (y+~30-50) — faster, good for checking your setup and getting ballpark Cl/Cd
- **Refined pass**: switch to Transition SST with y+~1 mesh once your domain/BCs/mesh strategy are validated, for more accurate results near your actual operating Re

## Boundary conditions — looks good, with a couple of additions

- **Velocity inlet, 30 m/s**: make sure you also set the **turbulence specification** here (Intensity + Viscosity Ratio is common default). For external aero, **turbulence intensity ~0.5-1%** (low, representing clean atmospheric/freestream flow) and **viscosity ratio ~5-10** is typical. Don't leave it at Fluent's default 5% intensity — that's tuned for internal flows and will over-predict turbulence levels in your freestream, affecting transition and separation prediction.
- **Pressure outlet, 0 gauge**: correct, and also set turbulence specification here too (same low intensity) in case of backflow during solution startup — prevents divergence if flow reverses momentarily at the outlet during early iterations.
- **Symmetry plane**: confirm it's actually set as type "Symmetry" not "Wall" in Fluent's BC list — this is a common mistake that silently ruins results without an obvious error.
- **Operating pressure**: check Fluent's operating pressure is set to 101325 Pa (standard atmospheric) if you're using gauge pressure = 0 at the outlet — this defines your reference.

## Hybrid initialization — good choice

Hybrid init gives a reasonable non-uniform starting guess (solves Laplace equation for velocity/pressure field) which converges faster and more robustly than standard initialization for external aero cases. No issues there.

## Residuals — default 10⁻³ is NOT enough for this

This is the part to be careful about:

- **Set convergence criteria to 10⁻⁶** for continuity, x/y/z-velocity, k, and omega — the Fluent default of 10⁻³ is too loose for aerodynamic force coefficients; you'll get a "converged" flag while Cl/Cd are still drifting.
- Better than relying on residuals alone: **monitor Cl and Cd directly** (Report Definitions → Lift/Drag coefficient monitors) and watch them **flatten out** over iterations — this is the real convergence indicator for aero cases, since residuals can plateau at a "good enough" level while force coefficients are still creeping.
- Also monitor **mass flow rate imbalance** between inlet and outlet — should approach zero as you converge.

## Additional solver settings worth setting before you run

- **Solution methods**: use **Coupled** scheme (faster convergence for steady RANS on external aero) rather than SIMPLE, if you have the memory for it. Second-order upwind for spatial discretization (momentum, turbulence quantities) — first-order is fine for the first ~50-100 iterations to stabilize, then switch to second-order for accuracy.
- **Number of iterations**: set high (2000-5000) and rely on your Cl/Cd monitors flattening + residuals hitting 10⁻⁶ to know when to stop, rather than assuming a fixed iteration count will converge.

## One thing to double check before running

Confirm your **reference values** (Reference Values panel) are set correctly — reference area (should be your **half-wing planform area**, not full wing, since you're using symmetry), reference length (root chord), and reference velocity (30 m/s) — Fluent uses these to compute Cl/Cd, and a wrong reference area is a very common silent error that gives believable-looking but wrong force coefficients.
